title: Minnesota lawyer suspended over fake AI case citations

reading.body:
The underlying article text was not available for review, so the specific facts of this incident, including the lawyer's name, the cases involved, the nature of the citations, and the details of the suspension, are not established here.

The title alone indicates a pattern seen in other documented incidents: a legal professional submitted court filings containing case citations that did not correspond to real decisions, with those citations attributed to AI-generated output. This is a failure mode in which a generative model produces plausible-looking but fabricated references, and a user relies on that output without independent verification against authoritative legal databases.

The point of failure in this pattern is not the model producing fiction, which is a known and documented behavior, but the absence of a checking step before the material reached a court. What would have caught it is the same verification any legal researcher would apply to a citation found in any secondary source: confirming the case exists and says what it is claimed to say.
